h1: The 7 Best Quiet Network Switches for Desks, Bedrooms and Media Closets in 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaTitle: Best Quiet Network Switches 2026: Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: 7 fanless network switches from TP-Link and NETGEAR, 5 and 8 port, gigabit and 2.5G, compared on ports, speed and value.
summary: The NETGEAR GS308 is the quiet switch to buy for most homes: eight gigabit ports, a fanless metal case and efficient Ethernet in a very low price bracket. The TP-Link TL-SG108S-M2 is the better pick if your internet or NAS has outgrown gigabit, and the TP-Link TL-SG105 is the five-port choice for a single desk. Every unit here is fanless, so the only thing you will hear is nothing.
intro: People shop for a quiet switch and then check the wrong thing. They read noise decibel figures that rarely exist, when the real answer is simpler: if a switch has no fan, it makes no fan noise. The ugly truth about cheap networking gear is that noise almost always comes from a small cooling fan in a managed or PoE model, not from an unmanaged box like these.

So this ranking is about everything else that separates a silent switch from a good one: port count, whether the ports run at 1 gigabit or 2.5 gigabit, how the metal case handles heat without airflow, and how the unit mounts on a desk or wall. We reviewed seven fanless unmanaged switches from the listings and spec sheets, and we did not measure sound.

products.name: NETGEAR GS308 8-Port Gigabit Unmanaged Switch
products.verdict: Eight gigabit ports in a fanless metal case, at a price almost everyone can justify.
products.description:
The GS308 is the default answer to a quiet home switch. It gives you eight gigabit ports in a fanless metal housing, supports 802.3az energy-efficient Ethernet, and can sit on a desk or mount to a wall. It sits in the under $25 bracket, which is remarkable for a metal-cased unit.

It ranks first because it covers the most common need, a handful of wired devices on a home network, without charging for features you will not use. Against the five-port GS305 it gives you three extra ports for the same kind of money, and extra ports are cheaper than a second switch later. The tradeoff is that gigabit speed is the ceiling, so it will not carry a multi-gig internet plan across your network.

Buy it if you have a router, a console, a desktop and a few other wired devices. Skip it if your ISP plan or NAS is faster than 1 gigabit.
pros: Eight ports for a tiny price
products.idealFor: Most homes with a router and several wired devices.
products.skipIf: You pay for a multi-gig internet plan.

products.name: TP-Link TL-SG108 8-Port Gigabit Unmanaged Switch
products.verdict: A shielded metal eight-port switch with 24x7 live technical support behind it.
products.description:
The TL-SG108 pairs eight gigabit ports with a shielded metal housing, a fanless design and plug-and-play setup, and TP-Link lists 24x7 live technical support alongside it. That support line is unusual for a budget switch and matters if you are the family IT person.

It ranks second only because the NETGEAR GS308 offers the same port count and the same silent design with the added mention of energy-efficient Ethernet and wall mounting, while the TP-Link does not list either in the facts we reviewed. The two are close in practice, and the shielded housing helps in rooms with a lot of electrical noise. Both sit under $25, so the pick comes down to brand preference.

Buy it if you like TP-Link's ecosystem or value a live support number. Skip it if you want a documented energy-saving mode.
pros: Eight ports in the lowest bracket
products.idealFor: Home networks where you want simple setup and a support line.
products.skipIf: Your uplink or storage is faster than gigabit.

products.name: TP-Link TL-SG108S-M2 8-Port 2.5G Unmanaged Switch
products.verdict: Eight 2.5G ports with 40Gbps of switching capacity, and it runs on the Cat5e you already have.
products.description:
The TL-SG108S-M2 gives you eight 2.5G ports and a stated 40Gbps switching capacity in a fanless unmanaged case. The key detail is that it works over existing Cat5e cabling, so the upgrade from gigabit does not require a rewire.

It ranks third because the extra speed only pays off if something on your network uses it: a 2.5G internet plan, a NAS, or a PC and router with 2.5G ports. For that buyer it is a sensible and quiet step up, and the $50 to $100 bracket is fair. For a household with gigabit everywhere, the cheaper GS308 above it delivers the same day-to-day experience.

Buy it if you already have 2.5G gear or plan to add it soon. Skip it if every device on your network is gigabit.
products.idealFor: Owners with a 2.5G internet plan, NAS or multi-gig PC.
products.skipIf: All your devices only support gigabit.

products.name: TP-Link TL-SG105 5-Port Gigabit Unmanaged Switch
products.verdict: A compact five-port switch with QoS, IGMP snooping and a three-year warranty.
products.description:
The TL-SG105 has five gigabit ports, QoS and IGMP snooping, a three-year warranty, and a metal case that works on a desk or a wall. It is the small-desk choice: a router at one end, a computer, a console, a printer and a spare port.

It ranks fourth because the eight-port models give you more room for the same money, but five ports is enough for a lot of people and the smaller body hides more easily. QoS and IGMP snooping are the interesting extras, and they help with video traffic and multicast streaming. The three-year warranty is the longest stated figure in this ranking, which counts as a durability signal.

Buy it if you have five or fewer wired devices and value the warranty. Skip it if you expect to add more wired gear soon.
products.idealFor: A compact desk with a handful of wired devices.
products.skipIf: You will outgrow five ports quickly.

products.name: NETGEAR GS305 5-Port Gigabit Unmanaged Switch
products.verdict: A fanless five-port switch with energy-efficient Ethernet for tight spaces.
products.description:
The GS305 is the five-port sibling of the GS308, sharing the fanless build and the power-saving Ethernet mode, and it sits on a shelf or screws to a wall. It sits in the under $25 bracket and is the smallest and simplest option in the group.

It ranks below the TL-SG105 because that model adds QoS, IGMP snooping and a stated three-year warranty, while this one keeps to the basics. It ranks above the larger multi-gig models for a buyer who only wants silence and gigabit, though the eight-port GS308 gives better room to grow. Treat it as the right size for one workstation or one entertainment shelf.

Buy it if you need to split one wall jack into several wired connections. Skip it if you want QoS features or more ports.
products.idealFor: A single desk or TV shelf needing a few more wired ports.
products.skipIf: You want QoS or room to expand.

products.name: TP-Link TL-SG105S-M2 5-Port 2.5G Unmanaged Switch
products.verdict: Five 2.5G ports and 25Gbps of capacity in a compact metal case, for $25 to $50.
products.description:
The TL-SG105S-M2 delivers five 2.5G ports with 25Gbps of switching capacity in a compact metal case, and it runs on existing Cat5e wiring. It is the cheapest way into multi-gig in this ranking, sitting in the $25 to $50 bracket.

It ranks sixth because a five-port 2.5G switch only makes sense if several of your devices have 2.5G ports, and most households do not yet. If you have one multi-gig PC and a router, you have a use for it. If you have a NAS plus workstation plus router, it is a strong pick. Otherwise the plain gigabit units below it in price give identical results for ordinary tasks.

Buy it if you have a small 2.5G setup and want to avoid spending on eight ports. Skip it if you do not own anything that benefits from multi-gig.
products.idealFor: A small setup with a few 2.5G devices.
products.skipIf: Your devices all top out at gigabit.

products.name: NETGEAR MS308 8-Port 2.5G Unmanaged Switch
products.verdict: A fanless eight-port 2.5G switch with efficient Ethernet, at the highest price here.
products.description:
The MS308 gives you eight 2.5G ports in a fanless design, works with existing Cat5e or Cat6 cabling, and supports 802.3az energy-efficient Ethernet. It is the most expensive unit here, sitting in the $100 to $200 bracket.

It ranks last, not because it is bad, but because the TP-Link TL-SG108S-M2 offers a comparable eight-port 2.5G setup for a lower price bracket and also states its 40Gbps switching capacity. The NETGEAR adds the energy-efficient Ethernet mention and a brand some owners trust for long-term firmware and support, which may justify the premium if you buy NETGEAR across your network.

Buy it if you want eight silent 2.5G ports and prefer NETGEAR. Skip it if price matters more than brand.
products.skipIf: You want the lowest price for eight 2.5G ports.

whatMatters.detail: A switch with no fan has no moving parts to make noise or wear out. The trade is that heat has to escape through the case, which is why metal housings are common on quiet models. Check the listing for the word fanless, because PoE and managed switches often add fans.

Gigabit ports top out at 1000 Mbps, while 2.5G ports reach 2500 Mbps over the same Cat5e cable. The speed only matters if the device at the other end can use it, so look at the Ethernet port on your router, NAS and PC before paying extra. A multi-gig switch connected to gigabit devices simply runs at gigabit.

Switching capacity is the total bandwidth the chip can move across all ports at once. For a simple eight-port home switch this is rarely the bottleneck, but stated figures such as the 25Gbps and 40Gbps on the TP-Link 2.5G units show the chip can keep every port busy. Check the listing for a stated number instead of assuming.

Unmanaged switches work out of the box with no configuration. Extras like QoS and IGMP snooping help prioritise video calls and multicast streams, but they are not a substitute for a managed switch with VLANs. Pick unmanaged for a plug-and-forget setup.

Many silent switches use a small external power adapter, so check where the outlet sits relative to the shelf or wall. Wall-mounting holes keep the switch off the desk and improve airflow around the metal case. Energy-efficient Ethernet also trims idle power draw.

faq.q: Will a quiet switch slow my internet?
faq.a: No. An unmanaged switch simply passes traffic between ports at wire speed. Your internet speed is limited by your plan and router, not by a switch with enough capacity.

faq.q: What is the common mistake when buying a switch?
faq.a: Buying multi-gig ports with no multi-gig devices. A 2.5G switch plugged into gigabit devices runs at gigabit, so check your router, NAS and PC ports first.

faq.q: Is a 2.5G switch worth it over a gigabit one?
faq.a: Only if you have gear that can use it, such as a 2.5G internet plan, a NAS or a modern motherboard. Otherwise the gigabit models do the same job for less and are just as silent.
Plug in the power adapter, connect your router to one port, and plug your devices into the rest. There is no software or configuration with these unmanaged models.

faq.q: Do these switches get hot without fans?
faq.a: They run warm to the touch, which is normal for a metal case that spreads heat. Give the switch some open space around it and avoid stacking items on top, especially in a closed cabinet.

faq.q: Can I use my existing Cat5e cables with 2.5G?
faq.a: Yes. The 2.5G switches here are listed as working over existing Cat5e cabling for typical home distances. Very long or poor-quality cable runs may drop to gigabit.

finalTake: The NETGEAR GS308 is the best quiet network switch for most people: eight silent gigabit ports, a metal case and wall mounting for very little money. The TP-Link TL-SG108 is a close second with live support, and the TP-Link TL-SG108S-M2 is the upgrade to buy when your internet or NAS goes multi-gig. Choose the five-port models only if you are sure you will never need a sixth cable.
